nominees.name: Isao Tanihata
nominees.affiliation: Research Center for Nuclear Physics, Osaka University, Japan; Beihang University, China

motivation: In 1985 Isao Tanihata, using pioneering radioactive-beam interaction cross-section measurements at Berkeley, found that Li-11 is anomalously large. In 1987 Björn Jonson, with the late P. Gregers Hansen, explained this as a neutron halo: weakly bound neutrons tunnelling far beyond the core, forming dilute, Borromean quantum systems. Jonson's subsequent ISOLDE and GSI experiments established the halo phenomenon across the drip lines. Together these discoveries overturned the picture of nuclei with a constant density and sharp surface, launched the worldwide programme of radioactive-beam facilities (RIKEN, FAIR, FRIB), and opened few-body and effective-field-theory descriptions of quantum halos with universal features shared with cold atoms. Today halo and drip-line nuclei are the most stringent tests of ab initio theory of how the strong force builds matter. This is a fundamental discovery whose impact keeps growing.
